item.title: The Duty of a Scholar
item.author: gslin
item.content:encoded:
On November 16th, 2004 — π years after arriving in Oxford — I submitted my doctoral thesis. My mind wasn't really on my thesis though; I was thinking about an issue I had noticed in recent Intel CPUs: The "Hyper-Threading" (simultaneous multithreading) feature they introduced in 2002 could leak information between execution threads via the cache state.
There was a joke at the time that although the National Security Agency had opened up in recent years and started taking their defensive role more seriously, the one aspect of cryptography which they would never discuss publicly was side channel attacks — and this itself constituted a side channel, revealing the importance they attributed to the field. Being active in computer security, and recognizing that the NSA knew a few things about the topic, my immediate priority was to determine whether the information leakage I had identified was sufficient to construct a practical cryptographic side channel. By mid-December I had a proof-of-concept exploit which stole enough bits of an RSA private key for the entire key to be reconstructed, and I turned my attention to the hard part of the problem: Quietly notifying security teams and working together to get the issue fixed before disclosing it publicly.
This became my occupation for the next six months. While my Oxonian contemporaries were making corrections to their theses and applying for jobs, I set those aside (much to the irritation of my supervisors): I had a responsibility, and it took priority over mere career considerations. As it turned out, being unemployed proved useful in early May, when Intel — rather irked by my impending publication — asked Yahoo to order me to withdraw the paper; Yahoo was very happy to reply that, unlike many FreeBSD developers, I was not in fact employed by them and they were not in a position to threaten to fire me. On May 13th, 2005, I presented my paper at BSDCan and published an advisory on the topic; advisories were published at the same time or soon thereafter by FreeBSD, NetBSD, Red Hat, SCO, and Ubuntu.
Anyone involved with open source software security will recognize the process of responsible disclosure (now widely called "coordinated disclosure", after some people in the industry struggled with the concept of responsibility), although the length of this particular process was unusual. If you find a security vulnerability, you shouldn't ignore it (or worse, sell it to bad actors); conversely, it's irresponsible to simply publish the vulnerability and hope that the good guys can fix it before the bad guys exploit it. Instead, you have a responsibility to identify who needs to know about the issue and to contact them — quietly — so they can get patches ready to distribute to their users the moment the issue becomes publicly known.
In this particular case, I was unusually able to put my life on hold: I was single, child-free, and, after defending my thesis and returning home to Canada, living rent-free in my (very tolerant) parents' basement. While I had some bills to cover — being a type 1 diabetic, I had to purchase insulin — living in Canada meant that I didn't need to worry about the risk of extraordinary costs from a hospital stay. Had I been living in the USA, I would have needed to prioritize seeking employment and medical insurance and likely would not have been able to discharge the duty which fate had thrust upon me.
Engineers, of course, are familiar with such duties: While the precise language varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, nearly all professional ethical codes include a requirement to act upon safety hazards regardless of whether any personal connection exists. Members of the IEEE commit, for example, "to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public..." without that duty being limited to hazards arising from projects employing the Engineer in question: The duty "to disclose promptly" vests in any Engineer who recognizes that the hazard exists. As with responsible disclosure of software security vulnerabilities, however, the subject matter of this duty is limited in scope: There is no duty to report if work is being done . As a legal duty this would be reasonable; but as a moral duty, I feel it sets the bar too low.
Engineering codes also often set out a process of escalation: In the common case of a licensed Engineer becoming aware of a hazard in a project they are working on, in the first instance they should report their concerns to their employer; only if that fails to yield results should they take more direct steps. This is both efficient and practical: Reporting an issue to someone who fails to act upon it isn't necessarily sufficient to discharge a duty, but conversely reporting everything broadly risks drowning out the few items which truly need broad attention. I routinely apply this same principle; for example, in 2009 I discovered that the Amazon EC2 firewall broke Path MTU Discovery by default and reported it to Amazon; but by November 2012 I concluded that Amazon was not going to address the problem, so I took to my blog to advise Amazon customers on how to fix Path MTU Discovery for themselves. (As it happened, Amazon fixed the bug a short time later.) While this was in no way a safety or computer security concern, I felt that, knowing what I did, I had an ethical duty to share that knowledge to help people who were affected by the issue.
In the Star Trek: The Next Generation episode "The First Duty", the late Patrick Stewart, speaking as Jean-Luc Picard, delivers a memorable speech about truth:
The first duty of every Starfleet officer is to the truth, whether it's scientific truth or historical truth or personal truth! It is the guiding principle on which Starfleet is based! If you can't find it within yourself to stand up and tell the truth about what happened, you don't deserve to wear that uniform!
The duty described here is a duty to uncover and not conceal the truth; while I agree with this duty, I don't think it goes far enough. To me, the duty includes actively seeking out people to whom the truth should be told. To hide behind "nobody asked" is to fail to fulfill the duty.
Much ink has been spilled by philosophers about duty and ethics, and the German Enlightenment philosopher Fichte in particular had some interesting comments to make in the fourth of his 1794 lectures, Über die Bestimmung des Gelehrten — often translated as The Vocation of the Scholar, which inspired the title of this essay. Fichte argues that Scholars have a particular relationship to knowledge: A Scholar "possesses his Knowledge not for himself, but for society". It is not proper for a Scholar to hoard knowledge; rather, Scholars have a duty to impart their knowledge to others — in Fichte's somewhat exaggerated view, to act as "the Teacher of the human race". On the other hand, it is unnecessary and inappropriate to enter with everyone into the "deep inquiries which he himself has been obliged to undertake"; rather, a Scholar relies upon others' trust in the Scholar's honesty when conveying the particular knowledge which is needed. Fichte notes that "[t]he Scholar will never be tempted to bring men to the adoption of his convictions by coercion or the use of physical force [...] neither will he deceive them". Scholars are not Plato's philosopher-kings; their duty is to provide the requisite knowledge, not to enforce what is done with that knowledge.
Now, I don't agree with Fichte on every point. Fichte considers Scholars to be the loftiest of all classes, and even invites each Scholar to consider themselves a "Priest of Truth"; living in rather more egalitarian times, I absolutely reject this framing. Nor do I accept Fichte's framing (in his preceding lecture, On the Distinction of Classes in Society) that the duty of Scholars to share knowledge arises from an obligation to render back to society what it has done for us; to me, the duty arises not from a debt to society, but rather attaches to knowledge itself, no matter who holds it.
This duty, naturally, is not unlimited. As Fichte notes, there is no duty to force people to act upon shared knowledge — indeed there is a moral obligation to accept everyone's freedom to choose how they act. Similarly, there is no duty to become a Cassandra: As with any gift, people are free to refuse the gift of knowledge, however unwise that might be; ultimately, if everyone who is able to act upon some knowledge has been made aware of it, the duty has been exhausted.
In modern vernacular, the terms "Scholar" and "Researcher" often overlap, but to me there is a very precise distinction: Researchers create new knowledge, while Scholars carry that knowledge to the people who need it — a narrower definition than that of Fichte, whose Scholars also carry a duty to strive to extend knowledge. Many people, of course, are both Researchers and Scholars; but there are plenty of people who perform research and publish papers without truly communicating their discoveries. The research paper which is published in a journal but never read is almost a cliché; but even papers which are read do not necessarily have the impact they deserve if they are read only by academics and not by anyone in a position to act upon the findings published. My undergraduate alma mater, Simon Fraser University — of which I have been a sitting Senator for over two decades — describes itself as "Canada's engaged university" and makes a point of valuing not just academic output but the work of connecting academic learning with the real world. A true Scholar, in my mind, is someone who feels bound by the duty of knowledge: To find the people with whom it should be shared.
It is for everyone to choose their own role in society, and not everyone feels every duty the same way; for that matter, just as my experience in 2005 would have been different had I needed to obtain medical insurance, not everyone is able to act upon a duty, no matter how much they feel it. But for myself, I choose the life and duty of a Scholar. blog comments powered by

item.content:encoded: Edit: Woah, this took off! If you want more details you can subscribe at the bottom of the post or on YouTube. I’m working on a more detailed highlights/commentary post and video.I got GPT-5.6 Sol, running in Codex with low thinking level, to complete a peaceful (i.e. no biters) Factorio run in 13.5 hours of game time:A timelapse of the full run is available on YouTube.Similar to my previous post, this run used a game manager to allow Sol/Codex to interact with the game via a small library (though in this run it was Python rather than Bash). The library allows the model to play the game programmatically while enforcing the same restrictions that human players face when using the GUI (e.g. reach of the player, fog of war).Observing the run was fascinating: Sol exceeded my expectations in some areas while also showing clear weaknesses in others. I have the entire run recorded and am working on a commentary video, but in the meantime here’s a small timelapsed segment showing some parts of the factory:Besides the screencast, my run manager also captured production statistics throughout the game. Here’s a chart of total resource production, annotated with science research milestones:I had planned to terminate the run after blue science research, but Sol’s surprising effectiveness convinced me to keep it going. Unfortunately, the scaling issues I thought would occur in the blue science stage appeared later and slowed Sol’s relative progress significantly.The rocket launch was only achieved through significant ‘manual’ effort on Sol’s part as it papered over its late-game failures to connect certain production systems by repeatedly ferrying supplies between areas of the factory.Still, I was pleased with the improvement over previous attempts with GPT-5.5 which suffered from the model’s failures to use transport belts at all.I’m optimistic about autonomous Factorio play as a medium for building intuition about the nature of model capabilities. In many ways playing Factorio is analogous to programming but with the benefit of being much more legible to casual observers, making it convenient for grounding discussion of model behaviors.I look forward to testing other models and thinking levels, as well as non-peaceful runs. Stay tuned!

item.title: Jepsen: ParticleDB 1.1.4
item.author: aphyr
item.content:encoded:
Modern applications often spread state across a variety of systems: databases, caches, queues, data warehouses, search indices, and so on. Coordinating these systems is challenging: caches are often stale, the analytics platform might lag days behind the primary database, the search index might lose data, and transactional updates across disparate systems remains an open research problem.ParticleDB aims to unify these workloads in a single engine with a special focus on AI agents and applications. It offers transactional SQL, a key-value store, vector search, live analytics, and user-defined functions called . To integrate with existing systems, clients can connect through a variety of interfaces, including the Postgres and Redis protocols, as well as its own gRPC and HTTP2 APIs. Written from the ground up in Rust, ParticleDB claims to be orders of magnitude faster than Postgres while preserving the same safety characteristics.ParticleDB was built by Orkes to support their workflow orchestration platform, Conductor. Conductor was initially built to store data in Redis and Postgres, but to improve performance, Orkes opted to write their own database. ParticleDB 1.0.0 offered a limited feature set specifically for Conductor’s queries, and was deployed as the backing database for some of their Conductor clusters. A few Orkes customers followed suit. In preparation for a broader release, Orkes undertook a major refactoring of ParticleDB, adding a custom wire protocol, more datatypes, additional OLAP queries, and more. While Orkes and their customers continued to run 1.0.0, they soft launched the refactored versions on particledb.ai. Orkes engaged Jepsen to test these versions of ParticleDB, beginning with 1.1.4.While ParticleDB could run as a single node, it also offered a replicated cluster using the Raft consensus protocol. This replication feature was available only in enterprise cloud deployments. The builds Orkes provided did not support replication, so this report covers only single-node behavior.ParticleDB’s home page advertised that ParticleDB was “formally proven” with a TLA+ proof. However, during our collaboration no TLA+ specification was available. It is unclear what properties might be proven, or whether they described ParticleDB as built.ParticleDB offered three tactics for syncing its Write-Ahead Log (WAL). The mode called on each commit, batched multiple transactions into a single , and skipped altogether. The Transaction Engine documentation described as offering “stronger durability” than . On the other hand, said the mode ensured that “COMMIT waits for flush”, and Orkes’ internal operator guide concurred: offered the “same durability as ”.ParticleDB’s home page proudly claimed “Full ACID. 159K TPS.” However, the text immediately below this said “snapshot isolation”, which is not fully isolated.Most SQL databases use the SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL statement to control the concurrent semantics of a transaction. However, ParticleDB ignored or rejected these statements. In some cases it instructed users to choose , a relatively weak isolation level. In other cases it accepted requests for different isolation levels, and silently ignored them (despite documentation to the contrary).Instead, transaction isolation was governed by the setting passed at startup. The transaction engine documentation described four modes:No locks; commit-on-writeBulk loads, single-writer benchmarksOverlay + commit-time OCC validation (default)General OLTP — safe under concurrencyPartition-pinned OCC; single-partition txns skip cross-partition coordinationHigh-throughput OLTP on partition-affine workloads (TPC-C, key-value)Exclusive table locks at first touchStrictest serialization, simple semanticsThis table was difficult to interpret. While the best practices documentation warned that users should “pick deliberately”, since “it changes correctness and throughput characteristics more than SQL text does”, the documentation did not explain what these modes actually guaranteed. The mode was clearly intended for weaker isolation, but was that Read Atomic, Read Uncommitted, or something else? The mode was similarly unclear. “Commit-time OCC validation” could describe a broad spectrum of consistency models from Read Uncommitted to Strong Serializable, but “safe under concurrency” suggests it might be Serializable. The mode described a performance optimization which could be as safe as , but it was described as “safe under concurrency”—raising the question: in what ways was it unsafe? Finally, if offered the “strictest serialization”, was some weaker isolation level?The CLI reference page contained another table which described and as “Jepsen-safe”, whereas was not “Jepsen-safe”, but did not explain their safety properties. Since Jepsen evaluates safety with respect to documentation and marketing claims, it is not clear how to interpret these terms.Running provided the following table:No locks, maximum OLTP throughput (unsafe under concurrency)Table locks + commit-time validation (safe for most OLTP)Partition-pinned OCC (highest throughput safe mode)Exclusive table locks, full serialization (strictest)Adaptive SSI (Cahill 2008), PL-3 with optimistic semantics (v1 scaffolding — see SSI_ADAPTIVE_DESIGN.md)The point of Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) is generally to taking locks, so the mention of table locks and a alias was surprising. Moreover, “safe for most OLTP” undermines the claim that was “safe under concurrency”; it suggests there are some OLTP workloads which are unsafe!Orkes explained that this documentation was wrong: was actually optimistic, and the alias was to preserve compatibility with an earlier two-phase locking mechanism. They also provided an unpublished operator guide with detailed descriptions of the various transaction modes. This document was difficult to interpret, but did specify the following consistency models: (a.k.a. , , ) (a.k.a. ) (a.k.a. ) (a.k.a. )Sources disagreed about the default transaction and WAL sync modes, but in general, and appeared to be the default.We wrote a test suite for ParticleDB using the Jepsen testing library. We ran ParticleDB versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 on individual Debian 13 nodes, both in containers and EC2 VMs. Our test harness could simulate process crashes by killing ParticleDB, simulate the loss of un-ed writes using LazyFS, and truncate or corrupt disk files. We ran ParticleDB using each transaction mode and all three WAL sync modes.We first tried ParticleDB’s official Java SDK. While the documentation indicated that the library was available as a Maven dependency, neither the JAR nor source code were actually available. Instead, we began with the official Postgres JDBC client, version 42.7.11, and later added support for the ParticleDB Java SDK, versions 1.0.0 through 1.0.2.We used several Jepsen workloads from other SQL databases, and designed new ones specifically for ParticleDB.The workload performed randomly generated transactions involving reads and writes of integer values identified by unique integer keys. We stored each value in a single row and accessed them both via primary and unindexed secondary keys. Keys and values were encoded as a variety of datatypes, including integers, decimals, and strings. We assumed that writes followed reads within each transaction, and that individual keys were sequentially consistent, and used these assumptions to infer constraints on the version orders and transaction dependency graphs. Jepsen’s transactional checker, Elle, then searched for cycles in that dependency graph, as well as a variety of non-cyclic phenomena like G1a (Aborted Read).The workload also performed randomly generated transactions over rows identified by unique integer keys, but the values were lists of integers. Transactions could read one of these lists by key, or append a unique integer to a list by key. We encoded each list as a comma-separated field, and used SQL to append to them. Rows could be selected via primary key or unindexed secondary key, or via a join to an indirection table. From there, we used Elle to infer version orders and dependency graphs, and searched for a variety of cyclic and non-cyclic phenomena.When these workloads revealed consistency violations within a single transaction, we designed an workload to stress internal consistency. This workload performed a series of randomly generated transactions involving , , , and statements over a simple key-value table, and verified that within each individual transaction, reads observed prior writes.To investigate tantalizing anomalies in the workload, we designed the workload. This workload used Clojure’s test.check generative testing library to produce random tables and simple SQL statements over them, then executed those statements against both ParticleDB and PostgreSQL. If ParticleDB’s behavior was not equivalent to PostgreSQL’s, the compare workload would search for a simpler sequence of statements that could reproduce the same divergence. Although our SQL generator was relatively simple—just a few basic datatypes, literals, arithmetic, comparisons, boolean logic, transactions, and some simple , , and clauses—it proved remarkably fruitful.Drawing on these successes, we devised a hybrid workload to search for violations of internal consistency in more complex transactions. This workload generated a random set of tables, then concurrently executed random transactions over them. It then checked each transaction independently to ensure that each of its statements observed results consistent with those preceding. For example, if a transaction executed , then observed a row with , we could prove that transaction was not internally consistent.We found 96 issues with ParticleDB, which we present in several categories below. All but three of these issues occurred in healthy, single-node instances of ParticleDB. Busy readers may wish to jump to the Discussion section, which summarizes our findings.Under normal operation, ParticleDB was slow, deadlocked, and crashed without warning.In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, was so slow as to be essentially unusable. While some transactions might complete in a few milliseconds, most took 10, 20, or even 30 seconds, then failed.For example, take this test run with a single node running 1.1.18.4, transaction mode , and WAL mode . With ten concurrent clients, most transactions blocked for tens of seconds before throwing could not serialize access due to concurrent update, or an IO error.High latencies (#62) appeared improved by 1.1.18.6, which could execute transactions with sub-100 millisecond latencies for at least a few seconds.While 1.1.18.6 improved latencies, it also crashed frequently. Crashes occurred spontaneously with various transaction modes, WAL modes, and client interfaces; there was no obvious cause. Nodes would run for a few hundred to a few thousand seconds before exiting. No error messages were printed. These crashes (#81) no longer appeared in 1.1.18.11.rc-18. Deadlock After Two Transactions (#27)In ParticleDB 1.1.18.8, submitting as few as two concurrent transactions to a healthy, single-node deployment could cause it to deadlock. This occurred both using the Postgres and ParticleDB interfaces. The node would log an error message like [DEADLOCK] 1 cycles detected at SystemTime ..., and an empty backtrace. In some cases new clients could attach and perform transactions; in others, new clients would also hang indefinitely. This may reflect multiple deadlock bugs.With the workload, version 1.1.18.9 generally could not run for more than 45 seconds without locking up. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 could reliably run for two minutes without lockups, and we declared the issue (#27) resolved. Deadlock With (#71)While version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 fixed the most frequent deadlocks, we continued to find deadlocks through 1.1.18.11.rc-6 when running with . An otherwise healthy ParticleDB node would execute transactions for about 30 seconds, then get stuck forever. The node would log a similar deadlock error message to #27, and all requests with the ParticleDB client would throw after a 100 second default timeout. These deadlocks (#71) appeared resolved by 1.1.18.11.rc-7.Orkes’ public documentation claimed broad support for Postgres features, and the internal operator guide concurred:The engine speaks PostgreSQL v3 wire protocol natively — anything that speaks pgjdbc / libpq / psycopg2 / pq connects unchanged. , , , prepared statements, parameterised queries, and extended-query pipelining all work as expected.These claims were somewhat optimistic. ParticleDB was missing support for a wide array of Postgres features, and others were badly broken. No Aggregates Within (#20)In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, aggregate expressions like were not supported within expressions.This threw Error: cannot evaluate wildcard expression. ParticleDB gained support for this feature (#20) by version 1.1.18.6. Unsupported Exponentiation (#28)ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 did not support the Postgres exponentiation operator:Version 1.1.18.9 added support for the operator (#28).In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9, any attempt to execute a prepared statement using the Postgres JDBC driver caused an exception like Execution error (NoSuchElementException) at java.util.ArrayDeque/removeFirst. The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Generative TestingThe workload generated random schemas and SQL statements over them, then ran both against ParticleDB and Postgres to see if they produced equivalent results. This should not have worked. There are many ways in which two “Postgres-compatible” databases can legitimately differ, such as floating-point details, which error message takes precedence, or the order of unsorted results. The space of SQL queries is large and difficult to cover. Many queries trivially return equivalent results (e.g. ) and therefore tell us little information. We can test only sequential behavior, which is easy for a database’s standard test suite to check.Nevertheless, roughly two thousand lines of generative tests found a wealth of bugs in ParticleDB, and unlike Jepsen’s typical workloads, the examples generated were usually easy to reproduce. ParticleDB offered a good deal of “low-hanging fruit” that should have been caught by example-based tests—but the workload also found more subtle errors. For example, the fact that was apparently equal to hinged on a high-precision floating-point literal. Inspired by this success, we extracted part of the ParticleDB SQL generator into a shared library so it could be used in other tests, like the new workload.Jepsen has traditionally focused on thorough analysis of a small set of carefully chosen transactions. This is partly because checking (e.g.) Serializability in general is NP-complete, and also because we assume that if transactions of (e.g.) reads and appends work correctly on strings, so will other operations on other datatypes. Our intuition is that the “hard part” is in the concurrency control mechanism, and sequential datatype behavior is generally covered by existing tests. This was not the case in ParticleDB. We’ve expanded Jepsen’s and tests to use alternate encodings and transaction structures, in an attempt to cover more codepaths. This revealed new bugs in ParticleDB, and we hope it will in other databases too.Unfortunately, became less useful as Orkes fixed major bugs and left smaller incompatibilities in place. For example, Postgres checks unique constraints when updating each row of a table, but ParticleDB only checks after all have been updated. This means that a statement like UPDATE bools SET x = NOT x can swap the values of and in ParticleDB without violating a unique constraint. Toward the end of our engagement, the test generally hit these minor inconsistencies early, then spent most of its time searching for minimal cases of them—potentially missing more serious bugs.Orkes said they ran Jepsen’s existing Postgres test harness to find and resolve issues in ParticleDB prior to this work. However, that same test harness failed immediately when run against ParticleDB 1.1.4. Orkes also stated they tested ParticleDB with SQLancer, which generates far more complex queries than the ones we tested. It is therefore perplexing that nearly every feature we tested exhibited glaring errors, and that our findings seemed to come as a surprise.Most databases have a test suite which exercises at least basic examples of each feature, and it is customary to run those tests before release, if not continuously. Where were those tests for ParticleDB? How does one add support for constraints without a test which tries to insert at least one value? What development process adds a type without trying to write a string of (e.g.) five characters?Our findings suggest structural deficiencies in the ParticleDB QA process. Perhaps tests were not run prior to release. Perhaps the test suite was run, but failed to exercise basic functionality. Perhaps engineers entrusted Large Language Models with the work of testing.Jepsen recommends that Orkes (and all database vendors!) build and exercise an automated test suite for their database. This suite should include at least simple, example-based tests covering important database features. These tests should fail when the feature is unimplemented or malformed, and pass when it is complete. Observing these failures is an important part of the development process: it validates that the test measures something. Tests should be run at least once before each release, and results disseminated to the team. Afterwards consider more sophisticated generative tests, establishing adversarial QA and implementation teams, and subtly breaking safety mechanisms to determine whether the tests are still effective.ParticleDB’s website gave the appearance of a mature database project. It made strong claims: a general-purpose OLTP/OLAP SQL database a thousand times faster than PostgreSQL, “formally verified” by a TLA+ proof, multiple APIs, and client libraries in thirteen languages. It offered a variety of deployment options and extensive documentation on database features and operations.On closer inspection, that documentation was riddled with omissions, inconsistencies, and confabulations. The TLA+ proof was not published, and in any event did not prevent disaster—perhaps it was incorrect, formalized the wrong properties, or did not describe the system as built. Safety-critical configuration settings like the transaction mode were described in vague terms, like “safe under concurrency”. The documentation for the Java client library referred to non-existent dependency coordinates and seemed to make up class and package names which were nowhere to be found in the library itself. The quickstart and client examples made up a variety of default usernames for ParticleDB, all of which were wrong. The stored procedure documentation even fabricated an imaginary email address for the author of this report. In Orkes’ unpublished operator guide, the descriptions of transaction modes omitted basic phenomena like G0 and confused G1a (Aborted Read) with G1c (Circular Information Flow). The Snapshot Isolation modes made no mention of G-single or the other boundary phenomena proscribed by Snapshot Isolation, and non-real-time models made no mention of the real-time phenomena they allowed, like Stale Read.Technical writing is important work that requires skill and care. Jepsen recommends that Orkes work with a human technical writer to rewrite ParticleDB’s documentation, with an eye toward concisely and accurately communicating intended behavior and the guarantees users should expect.Jepsen is no stranger to working with early software projects, and there is nothing intrinsically wrong with offering buggy or badly broken software. However, it would be polite for a maintainer aware of serious safety issues to display a prominent warning on the website. One might place a large red box on the download page which reads, “This project is in early development and is not suitable for production”, or more bluntly, “This software has lost data and will do so again”. It is not clear how users would have understood versions like 1.1.4 or 1.1.18.9 as “pre-release”. Pre-release software generally has a version number beginning with 0, or including “rc”, “alpha”, etc. The documentation did not describe these versions as pre-release or experimental at the time. Indeed, the Docker install page told users how to deploy these versions “for production”.Large Language Models enable small teams to produce software and documentation of staggering scope and complexity in a remarkably short time. Five years ago, writing a distributed SQL database of this scope might have taken hundreds of person-years. With LLM assistance, a handful of engineers at Orkes were able to produce a highly sophisticated database system.However, our work on ParticleDB (and other databases) suggests there are serious tradeoffs to relying on LLMs. Quality suffered: ParticleDB was a fractal of correctness errors. LLM tooling repeatedly claimed that bugs had been fixed when, in fact, they had not. ParticleDB also seemed more difficult to understand than typical databases. As with most Jepsen analyses, Orkes engineers offered detailed explanations of the causes and resolutions of the bugs we found in Conductor. However, Orkes seemed unable to explain the causes or resolutions of nearly every issue we found in ParticleDB. New builds simply materialized, sans changelogs, each hopefully containing a slew of improvements. Why did ParticleDB sometimes turn strings into integers? Why did it stop in 1.1.18.11.rc-1? Perhaps no one knows. With LLMs, perhaps no one needs to.More broadly, the use of LLMs erodes trust in documentation, in software, and in the organizations which produce them. Perhaps engineers will begin to treat any new software project with suspicion—the signals we used to rely on as markers of a mature system are now easier to counterfeit.Where correctness matters—and surely it ought to matter for databases!—our industry must acknowledge and mitigate these tradeoffs. In the age of LLMs, what can maintainers do to ensure correct software and accurate documentation? Having done that work, how can they demonstrate its quality to users?As of 1.1.18.11.rc-22, our and workloads were still finding anomalies in every transaction mode.
